Sodomites
SOD-om-ites
n. pl.
From Sodom, the city destroyed in Genesis 19, with the suffix -ite. Webster 1828 defines sodomy from the crime of Sodom. In the Authorized Version the word renders Hebrew qadesh, a male cult prostitute attached to the pagan shrines.

Biblical Definition

Sodomites in the Authorized Version renders the Hebrew qadesh — literally a consecrated one — the male shrine prostitutes belonging to the fertility cults of Canaan. The law forbids their existence in Israel outright: There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:17). The historical books then measure kings by whether they removed them. Under Rehoboam they entered the land: there were also sodomites in the land: and they did according to all the abominations of the nations which the LORD cast out before the children of Israel (1 Kings 14:24). Asa is commended for the purge: he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made (1 Kings 15:12). Jehoshaphat completed it: the remnant of the sodomites, which remained in the days of his father Asa, he took out of the land (1 Kings 22:46). The name reaches back to Genesis 19, where the men of the city surrounded Lot’s house demanding his guests, and Jude describes the cities as giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh (Jude 1:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 traces SODOMY and its derivatives to the crime of the city of Sodom. In the Authorized Version the plural noun renders the Hebrew term for the male cult prostitutes of the Canaanite shrines, whose presence in Israel the law forbade and whose removal marks the reforming kings.

expand to see more

SODOMITE, n. — One guilty of the crime named from the city of Sodom; in the Authorized Version, a male temple prostitute of the Canaanite religion.

The Hebrew word is qadesh, a consecrated one — consecrated to a false deity, and so the exact inversion of holiness.

The presence or removal of such persons is used in Kings as a measure of a reign’s fidelity.

SODOM, n. — The city of the plain destroyed by fire from heaven in the days of Abraham and Lot.

From the proper name Sodom, with the gentilic suffix -ite, denoting one belonging to or characterised by it.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 23:17 — "There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel."

1 Kings 14:24 — "And there were also sodomites in the land: and they did according to all the abominations of the nations which the LORD cast out before the children of Israel."

1 Kings 15:12 — "And he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made."

1 Kings 22:46 — "And the remnant of the sodomites, which remained in the days of his father Asa, he took out of the land."

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

Modern Corruption

Affirming theology has attempted to confine these texts to cult prostitution, exploitation, or inhospitality, so that Scripture is said to say nothing about the conduct itself — a reading Romans 1 forecloses by grounding the prohibition in creation rather than in culture.

expand to see more

The revisionist argument runs that the Old Testament texts concern shrine prostitution, that Sodom’s sin was inhospitality (citing Ezekiel 16:49), and that Paul addresses exploitative Greco-Roman practices rather than the conduct as such. Each claim founders on the texts. Ezekiel 16:50 finishes the sentence the revisionist reading stops in the middle of: they were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away as I saw good. Jude 1:7 names the sin of the cities as going after strange flesh. And Romans 1:26-27 does not appeal to any local custom or to any imbalance of power; it appeals to nature and to creation, saying that women did change the natural use into that which is against nature and that men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another. Leviticus 18 and 20 place the prohibition among laws binding on the resident foreigner too, which marks them as more than ceremonial.

Two things must be said with equal firmness, and the dictionary says both. First, the imago Dei is entire in every person, and Genesis 1:27 is not qualified by anyone’s conduct or desires; contempt, cruelty, and the treatment of any person as a category rather than a soul are themselves sins, and churches have committed them. Second, 1 Corinthians 6:11 is the verse that settles the tone of the whole matter. Paul lists the fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, effeminate, abusers of themselves with mankind, thieves, covetous, drunkards, revilers and extortioners — and then writes, And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified. The past tense is the gospel. There were such people in the Corinthian church, and they had been washed; the same door stands open, and no other door does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qadesh (H6945), a male cult prostitute, from qadash, to be set apart; qedeshah (H6948), the female counterpart; toebah (H8441), an abomination; Greek arsenokoites (G733), coined by Paul from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22.

expand to see more

Hebrew qadesh (H6945) — a consecrated one, a male shrine prostitute; the word rendered sodomite (Deuteronomy 23:17).

Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to be set apart, consecrated; the same root as holy, which makes the term a deliberate inversion.

Hebrew toebah (H8441) — an abomination, a detestable thing; the standing verdict of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.

Greek arsenokoites (G733) — literally male-bedder; Paul appears to have coined it from the Septuagint wording of Leviticus 18:22 (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10).

Greek para phusin — against nature; the phrase of Romans 1:26, appealing to creation rather than custom.

Usage

"Nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:17) — the law’s flat prohibition."

"He took away the sodomites out of the land (1 Kings 15:12) — the measure by which Kings weighs a reforming reign."

"And such were some of you: but ye are washed (1 Corinthians 6:11) — the past tense that is the gospel."
